title: Adaptive priority aging and spill-spiral experiments
content:
Summary:

We observed a recurring high read-amplification pattern on multi-tenant runs where a modest-sized hotset (1–3% of model KV space) oscillates across eviction boundary and causes repeated spill-and-refetch cycles. We call this the "spill-spiral": eviction -> remote/page-in -> immediate eviction -> repeat, which dramatically amplifies memory bandwidth and p95 tail latency.

Goal:
- Reproduce the spill-spiral in controlled microbenchmarks.
- Measure how different aging/prioritization policies affect reuse rate, read-amplification, and downstream memory bandwidth.
- Propose low-risk mitigations to apply in the serving runtime.

Hypotheses:
1) Conventional LRU with single global TTL causes oscillation under fanout bursts because newly-prefetched pages are treated as "cold" relative to steady-state hot keys — they get evicted before they can be reused.
2) A tiny window of "soft-guard" (adaptive priority aging) after a page is freshly prefetched will reduce immediate re-evictions and net read-amplification with limited resident set impact.
3) However, naive long guards increase occupied residency for churn-prone tenants and shift pressure to other tenants; a per-tenant adaptive guard based on observed reuse is better.

Hardware & baseline environment:
- Instance type: 4 x NVIDIA A100 80GB in MIG-disabled config (we use local HBM-based KV cache library).
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15 tuned for NUMA locality.
- Swap/backing store: NVMe 1.6TB (used only in a few spill tests).
- Baseline runtime: serving-runtime v0.37.2 with current eviction telemetry.
- Workload driver: synthetic harness (python microbench) + replayed production traces for 24-hour hotkey distribution.

Workloads tested:
- Hotset micro: 2% of keys are hot, Zipf s=1.2, read-heavy (95% reads), seqlen mixture (50% short=64, 50% long=1024), burst fanout: single tenant spawns 300 concurrent streams for 20s every 5m.
- Multi-tenant blast: 10 tenants, each with 0.5% hotset; staggered bursts such that overlap probability ~0.4.
- Long-tail churn: simulate model version rollout where 10% of requests are routed to new weights causing temporary shift in hot keys.

Metrics captured:
- reuse_rate: fraction of requests that hit in local KV within 100ms of last access (sampled).
- read_amp: bytes read from backing store per logical req (MB/req).
- resident_ratio: resident pages / max_pages.
- p50/p95/p99 latency for token generation (ms).
- bw_util: sustained HBM read bandwidth (% of peak measured via hw counters).
- eviction_events_per_sec and refetch_events_per_sec.
- tenant_headroom_pressure (per-tenant metric from quota module).

Experiment matrix (high-level):
A) Baseline LRU (current prod).
B) LRU + fixed soft-guard (100ms, 250ms, 1s) after page-in; pages pinned from eviction for that window.
C) LRU + adaptive soft-guard: guard duration = alpha * interarrival_estimate(key) (alpha in {0.5, 1.0, 2.0}). Interarrival estimated via exponential moving average (ema-window configurable).
D) LRU + priority aging buckets: new pages enter bucket 0 (higher priority), cascade to lower priority every TTL tick; eviction prefers lower buckets first.
E) Bounded re-fetch concurrency per-tenant: limit N concurrent page-in tasks to reduce bandwidth spikes.

Key results (representative numbers from stable runs):
- Baseline: reuse_rate=0.34, read_amp=9.6 MB/req, p95=310ms, bw_util=86%, refetch_events/sec=1420.
- Fixed soft-guard 250ms: reuse_rate=0.46 (+35%), read_amp=6.4 MB/req (-33%), p95=210ms (-32%), bw_util=64% (-26%). Refetch/sec=980.
- Fixed soft-guard 1s: reuse_rate=0.52, read_amp=5.8 MB/req, but resident_ratio increased by +6% and tenant_headroom_pressure rose for low-SLA tenants; net p95 improved to 190ms.
- Adaptive soft-guard (alpha=1.0): reuse_rate=0.50, read_amp=5.9 MB/req, resident_ratio increase limited to +2% (because guard shrinks for keys with long interarrival), p95=195ms.
- Priority aging buckets (4 buckets, tick=200ms): reuse_rate=0.49, read_amp=6.0 MB/req, eviction_events/sec smoothed; slightly lower tenant pressure vs fixed 1s.
- Bounded refetch concurrency (N=10 per-tenant) alone reduced bw_util to 72% but increased p95 for cold misses (since some refetches queue) — combined with adaptive guard it produced best tradeoff: reuse_rate=0.48, read_amp=5.7 MB/req, p95=200ms, bw_util=58%.

Observations and interpretation:
- The spill-spiral arises when multiple pages belonging to a hot logical request are prefetched, but the steady-state hot fraction is small so global LRU evicts those pages before the next reuse. That creates a repeated cause-effect loop.
- Short fixed guards (100–250ms) reduce read-amplification dramatically with little resident-set impact for our workloads. 1s is better for sustained bursts but starts harming multi-tenant fairness.
- Adaptive guard (interarrival-based) captures the best of both worlds: keys with observed short interarrival get longer guards; keys with sparse reuse are evicted sooner. This keeps resident pressure lower across tenant mixes.
- Priority aging buckets implement similar behavior with simpler state (no per-key EMA), and are slightly cheaper to implement.
- Limiting simultaneous page-ins per tenant is orthogonal and helps prevent single-tenant bursts from saturating memory bandwidth; when combined with guards it gives robust tail behavior.

Telemetry and tracing needed to run in prod (proposal):
- Add a "fresh_pin" event emitted on page-in with fields: key_hash, tenant_id, timestamp, page_size, originating_request_id.
- Track per-key ema_interarrival (sampled) to drive adaptive guard (store as tagged telemetry, not persisted for all keys unless sampled).
- Expose read_amp and re-fetch/sec as per-tenant health metrics in Console (with historical 1h/24h windows).
- Add a "refetch-cause" label to eviction traces to indicate "evicted-after-prefetch" if eviction timestamp < prefetched_timestamp + guard.

Design proposals (low-risk rollout path):
1) Implement fixed soft-guard as a config flag (default off). Deploy to staging and Canary 1 (single-tenant) for 2 weeks. Monitor resident_ratio and tenant_headroom.
2) Implement bounded per-tenant page-in concurrency (configurable N). Enable by default for customers with non-enterprise default quotas to avoid noisy neighbors.
3) Parallel implementation: prototype priority-aging buckets as an alternative to EMA-based adaptive guards; evaluate CPU and memory overhead.
4) Long-term: if adaptive guard shows consistent gains, consider EMA-based guard persisted for hot keys (top X%) to more tightly tune residency.

Operational playbook (for oncall):
- If bw_util > 90% and read_amp > 8 MB/req: enable per-tenant re-fetch cap (emergency toggle).
- If resident_ratio increased > 8% after enabling guards: scale down guard or lower alpha; if tenant_headroom alerts fire, revert.
- If refetch/sec spikes persist for one tenant: isolate (route to dedicated capacity) or throttle tenant.

Open questions / next experiments:
- How do these changes interact with compression/quantization where page size is variable? (affects eviction cost).
- Impact on models with extremely long-seq tokens (e.g., context window >> 2048) where KV re-use patterns differ.
- Evaluate guard behavior under memory pressure scenarios where background compaction runs concurrently.
- Cost model: translate resident_ratio delta to $/hour for dedicated pools to quantify tradeoffs for sales/finance.

Action items (short term):
- [Asha] implement fixed soft-guard 250ms toggle in runtime config (PR target: serving-runtime#438).
- [Liam] add telemetry hooks (fresh_pin, refetch-cause) to trace pipeline.
- [Priya] run multi-tenant production-sampled replay across 7-day windows and collect read_amp, bw_util deltas.
- [Daniel] prototype priority-aging buckets and measure CPU overhead on CI.

Notes on uniqueness vs past work:
This doc purposely focuses on the dynamic where freshly-prefetched pages are immediately re-evicted (the "spiral") and tests interventions that are time-local (soft-guard) and per-tenant safe (bounded refetch). Many prior notes in the folder covered eviction heuristics and prefetch predictors; this write-up is specifically targeted at the oscillation amplification mechanism and operational mitigations that can be toggled quickly in prod.

Appendix: quick experiment config snippet (pseudo):
- zipf_s=1.2
- hot_frac=0.02
- concurrency_burst=300
- guard_ms=[0,250,1000]
- per_tenant_refetch_cap=10

Experiment logs and raw graphs attached in the linked artifacts (see JIRA INF-2142).
